{{Short description|Logarithm of a complex number}}

[[Image:Complex log domain.svg|200px|thumb|A single branch of the complex logarithm. The [[hue]] of the color is used to show the [[Argument (complex analysis)|argument]] of the complex logarithm. The brightness of the color is used to show the [[modulus of a complex number|modulus]] of the complex logarithm. ]]
[[Image:NaturalLogarithmRe.png|200px|thumb|The real part of {{math|log(z)}} is the [[natural logarithm]] of {{math|{{abs|''z''}}}}. Its [[graph of a function|graph]] is thus obtained by rotating the graph of {{math|ln(''x'')}} around the [[z-axis|{{mvar|z}}-axis]].]]

In [[mathematics]], a '''complex logarithm''' is a generalization of the [[natural logarithm]] to nonzero [[complex number]]s. The term refers to one of the following, which are strongly related:
* A complex logarithm of a nonzero complex number <math>z</math>, defined to be any complex number <math>w</math> for which <math>e^w = z</math>.<ref name=Ahlfors>Ahlfors, Section 3.4.</ref><ref name=Sarason>Sarason, Section IV.9.</ref>  Such a number <math>w
</math> is denoted by <math>\log z</math>.<ref name=Ahlfors/>  If <math>z</math> is given in [[polar form]] as <math>z = re^{i\theta}</math>, where <math>r</math> and <math>\theta</math> are real numbers with <math>r>0</math>, then <math>\ln r + i \theta</math> is one logarithm of <math>z</math>, and all the complex logarithms of <math>z</math> are exactly the numbers of the form <math>\ln r + i\left(\theta + 2\pi k\right)</math> for integers <math>k</math>.<ref name=Ahlfors/><ref name=Sarason/>  These logarithms are equally spaced along a vertical line in the complex plane.
* A complex-valued function <math>\log \colon U \to \mathbb{C}</math>, defined on some subset <math>U</math> of the set <math>\mathbb{C}^*</math> of nonzero complex numbers, satisfying <math>e^{\log z} = z</math> for all <math>z</math> in <math>U</math>.  Such complex logarithm functions are analogous to the real [[natural logarithm|logarithm function]] <math>\ln \colon \mathbb{R}_{>0} \to \mathbb{R}</math>, which is the [[inverse function|inverse ]] of the real [[exponential function]] and hence satisfies  {{math|''e''<sup>ln ''x''</sup> {{=}} ''x''}} for all [[positive real numbers]] {{mvar|x}}.  Complex logarithm functions can be constructed by explicit formulas involving real-valued functions, by integration of <math>1/z</math>, or by the process of [[analytic continuation]].  

There is no [[continuous function|continuous]] complex logarithm function defined on all of <math>\mathbb{C}^*</math>.  Ways of dealing with this include [[branch point|branches]], the associated [[Riemann surface]], and [[partial inverse]]s of the [[Exponential function#Complex plane|complex exponential function]].  The ''principal value'' defines a particular complex logarithm function <math>\operatorname{Log} \colon \mathbb{C}^* \to \mathbb{C}</math> that is continuous except along the negative real axis; on the [[complex plane]] with the negative real numbers and 0 removed, it is the [[analytic continuation]] of the (real) natural logarithm.

==Problems with inverting the complex exponential function==
[[File:Riemann surface log.svg|thumb|right|A plot of the multi-valued imaginary part of the complex logarithm function, which shows the branches. As a complex number {{math|''z''}} goes around the origin, the imaginary part of the logarithm goes up or down. This makes the origin a [[branch point]] of the function.]]

For a function to have an inverse, it must [[Injective function|map distinct values to distinct values]]; that is, it must be [[injective]]. But the complex exponential function is not injective, because <math>e^{w+2\pi i k} = e^w</math> for any complex number <math>w</math> and [[integer]] <math>k</math>, since adding <math>i \theta</math> to <math>z</math> has the effect of rotating <math>e^w</math> counterclockwise <math>\theta</math> [[radian]]s. So the points
<math display="block">\ldots,\;w-4\pi i, \;w-2\pi i, \;w, \;w + 2\pi i, \;w+4\pi i, \;\ldots,</math>
equally spaced along a vertical line, are all mapped to the same number by the exponential function.  This means that the exponential function does not have an inverse function in the standard sense.<ref>Conway, p. 39.</ref><ref>Another interpretation of this is that the "inverse" of the complex exponential function is a [[multivalued function]] taking each nonzero complex number {{math|''z''}} to the ''set'' of all logarithms of {{math|''z''}}.</ref>  There are two solutions to this problem.

One is to restrict the domain of the exponential function to a region that does not contain any two numbers differing by an integer multiple of <math>2\mathit{\pi i}</math>: this leads naturally to the definition of [[branch cut|branches]] of <math>\log z</math>, which are certain functions that single out one logarithm of each number in their domains. This is analogous to the definition of <math>\arcsin x</math> on <math>[-1, 1]</math> as the inverse of the restriction of <math>\sin \theta</math> to the interval <math>[-\pi/2, \pi/2]</math>: there are infinitely many real numbers <math>\theta</math> with <math>\sin \theta = x</math>, but one arbitrarily chooses the one in <math>[-\pi/2, \pi/2]</math>.

Another way to resolve the indeterminacy is to view the logarithm as a function whose domain is not a region in the [[complex plane]], but a Riemann surface that [[covering space|covers]] the punctured complex plane in an infinite-to-1 way.

Branches have the advantage that they can be evaluated at complex numbers. On the other hand, the function on the Riemann surface is elegant in that it packages together all branches of the logarithm and does not require an arbitrary choice as part of its definition.

==Principal value==

===Definition===
For each nonzero complex number <math>z</math>, the ''principal value'' <math>\operatorname{Log} z</math> is the logarithm whose [[imaginary part]] lies in the interval <math>(-\pi, \pi]</math>.<ref name=Sarason/> The expression <math>\operatorname{Log} 0</math> is left undefined since there is no complex number <math>w</math> satisfying <math>e^w = 0</math>.<ref name=Ahlfors/>

When the notation <math>\log z</math> appears without any particular logarithm having been specified, it is generally best to assume that the principal value is intended. In particular, this gives a value consistent with the real value of <math>\ln z</math> when <math>z</math> is a positive real number. The capitalization in the notation <math>\text{Log}</math> is used by some authors<ref name=Sarason/> to distinguish the principal value from other logarithms of <math>z.</math>

===Calculating the principal value===
The [[polar form]] of a nonzero complex number <math>z= x + yi</math> is  <math>z=re^{i\theta}</math>, where <math DISPLAY=inline>r = |z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}</math> is the [[absolute value]] of <math>z</math>, and <math>\theta</math> is its [[argument (complex analysis)|argument]]. The absolute value is real and positive. The argument is defined  [[up to]] addition of an integer multiple of {{math|2{{pi}}}}. Its [[Argument (complex analysis)#Principal value|principal value]] is the value that belongs to the [[interval (mathematics)|interval]] <math>(-\pi, \pi]</math>, which is expressed as [[atan2|<math>\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)</math>]].

This leads to the following formula for the principal value of the complex logarithm:
<math display="block">\operatorname{Log} z = \ln r + i \theta = \ln |z| + i \operatorname{Arg} z = \ln\sqrt{x^2+y^2} + i \operatorname{atan2}(y,x).</math>
For example, <math>\operatorname{Log}(-3i) = \ln 3 - \pi i/2</math>, and <math>\operatorname{Log}(-3) = \ln 3 + \pi i</math>.

===The principal value as an inverse function===
Another way to describe <math>\operatorname{Log} z</math> is as the inverse of a restriction of the complex exponential function, as in the previous section. The horizontal strip <math>S</math> consisting of complex numbers <math>w = x + yi</math> such that <math>-\pi < y \le \pi</math> is an example of a region not containing any two numbers differing by an integer multiple of <math>2\pi i</math>, so the restriction of the exponential function to <math>S</math> has an inverse. In fact, the exponential function maps <math>S</math> [[bijection|bijectively]] to the punctured complex plane <math>\mathbb{C}^* = \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}</math>, and the inverse of this restriction is <math>\operatorname{Log}\colon \mathbb{C}^* \to S</math>. The conformal mapping section below explains the geometric properties of this map in more detail.

===The principal value as an analytic continuation===
On the region <math>\mathbb{C} - \mathbb{R}_{\le 0}</math> consisting of complex numbers that are not negative real numbers or 0, the function <math>\operatorname{Log} z</math> is the [[analytic continuation]] of the natural logarithm.  The values on the negative real line can be obtained as limits of values at nearby complex numbers with positive imaginary parts.

===Properties===
Not all identities satisfied by <math>\ln</math> extend to complex numbers. It is true that <math>e^{\operatorname{Log} z} = z</math> for all <math>z \neq 0</math> (this is what it means for <math>\operatorname{Log} z</math> to be a logarithm of <math>z</math>), but the identity <math>\operatorname{Log} (e^z) = z</math> fails for <math>z</math> outside the strip <math>S</math>. For this reason, one cannot always apply <math>\text{Log}</math> to both sides of an identity <math>e^z = e^w</math> to deduce <math>z = w</math>. Also, the identity <math>\operatorname{Log}(z_1 z_2) = \operatorname{Log}z_1 + \operatorname{Log}z_2</math> can fail: the two sides can differ by an integer multiple of <math>2 \pi i</math>;<ref name=Ahlfors/> for instance,
<math display="block">\operatorname{Log}((-1)i) = \operatorname{Log}(-i) = \ln(1) -\frac{\pi i}{2} = -\frac{\pi i}{2}, </math>
but
<math display="block">\operatorname{Log}(-1) + \operatorname{Log}(i) = \left( \ln(1) + \pi i \right) + \left( \ln(1) + \frac{\pi i}{2} \right) = \frac{3\pi i}{2} \ne -\frac{\pi i}{2}.</math>

The function <math>\operatorname{Log} z</math> is discontinuous at each negative real number, but continuous everywhere else in <math>\mathbb{C}^*</math>. To explain the discontinuity, consider what happens to <math>\arg z</math> as <math>z</math> approaches a negative real number <math>a</math>. If <math>z</math> approaches <math>a</math> from above, then <math>\arg z</math> approaches <math>\pi,</math> which is also the value of <math>\arg a</math> itself. But if <math>z</math> approaches <math>a</math> from below, then <math>\arg z</math> approaches <math>-\pi.</math> So <math>\arg z</math> "jumps" by <math>2\pi</math> as <math>z</math> crosses the negative real axis, and similarly <math>\operatorname{Log} z</math> jumps by <math>2 \pi i.</math>

==Branches of the complex logarithm==
Is there a different way to choose a logarithm of each nonzero complex number so as to make a function <math>\operatorname{L} (z)</math> that is continuous on all of <math>\mathbb{C}^*</math>? The answer is no. To see why, imagine tracking such a logarithm function along the [[unit circle]], by evaluating <math>\operatorname{L} \left( e^{i\theta} \right)</math> as <math>\theta</math> increases from <math>0</math> to <math>2\pi</math>.  If <math>\operatorname{L} (z)</math> is continuous, then so is <math>\operatorname{L} \left( e^{i\theta} \right) - i \theta</math>, but the latter is a difference of two logarithms of <math>e^{i\theta},</math> so it takes values in the discrete set <math>2\pi i \mathbb{Z},</math> so it is constant. In particular, <math>\operatorname{L} \left( e^{2\pi i} \right) - 2\pi i =  \operatorname{L} \left( e^0 \right) - 0</math>, which contradicts <math>\operatorname{L} \left( e^{2\pi i} \right) =  \operatorname{L} \left( e^0 \right) </math>.

To obtain a continuous logarithm defined on complex numbers, it is hence necessary to restrict the domain to a smaller subset <math>U</math> of the complex plane. Because one of the goals is to be able to [[derivative|differentiate]] the function, it is reasonable to assume that the function is defined on a neighborhood of each point of its domain; in other words, <math>U</math> should be an [[open set]]. Also, it is reasonable to assume that <math>U</math> is [[Connectedness|connected]], since otherwise the function values on different components of <math>U</math> could be unrelated to each other. All this motivates the following definition:

{{block indent | left = 1.6 | text = <p>A ''branch'' of <math>\log z</math> is a continuous function <math>\operatorname{L} (z)</math> defined on a connected open subset <math>U</math> of the complex plane such that <math>\operatorname{L} (z)</math> is a logarithm of <math>z</math> for each <math>z</math> in <math>U</math>.<ref name=Sarason /></p>}}

For example, the principal value defines a branch on the open set where it is continuous, which is the set <math>\mathbb{C}-\mathbb{R}_{\le 0}</math> obtained by removing 0 and all negative real numbers from the complex plane.

Another example: The [[Mercator series]]
<math display="block">
\ln(1+u)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n} u^n
= u - \frac{u^2}{2} + \frac{u^3}{3} - \cdots
</math>
[[Convergent series|converges]] [[uniform convergence|locally uniformly]] for <math>|u| < 1</math>, so setting <math>z = 1 + u</math> defines a branch of <math>\log z</math> on the open disk of radius 1 centered at 1. (Actually, this is just a restriction of <math>\operatorname{Log} z</math>, as can be shown by differentiating the difference and comparing values at 1.)

Once a branch is fixed, it may be denoted <math>\log z</math> if no confusion can result. Different branches can give different values for the logarithm of a particular complex number, however, so a branch must be fixed in advance (or else the [[principal branch]] must be understood) in order for "<math>\log z</math>" to have a precise unambiguous meaning.

In some literature, the notation <math>\ln_k z</math> is used to explicitly denote the <math>k</math>-th branch of the complex logarithm. This notation is particularly useful when working with multi-valued logarithms in complex analysis and topology. It was first introduced in the paper ''Unwinding the Branches of the Lambert W function''<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jeffrrey |first1=D.J. |last2=Hare |first2=D.E.G. |last3=Corless |first3=Robert M. |date=1996 |title=Unwinding the branches of the Lambert W function |url=https://www.uwo.ca/apmaths/faculty/jeffrey/pdfs/wbranch.pdf |journal=The Mathematical Scientist |volume=21 |pages=1–7}}</ref> and was later referenced in the work of [https://www.math.uwo.ca/faculty/jeffrey_david/index.html David Jeffrey].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Calkin |first1=Neil J. |title=Computational Discovery on Jupyter |last2=Chan |first2=Eunice Y. S. |last3=Corless |first3=Robert M. |publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics |year=2023 |isbn=978-1-61197-749-3}}</ref>

===Branch cuts===
The argument above involving the unit circle generalizes to show that no branch of <math>\log z</math> exists on an open set <math>U</math> containing a [[closed curve]] that [[winding number|winds]] around 0. One says that <math>\log z</math> has a ''[[branch point]] at 0''.  To avoid containing closed curves winding around 0, <math>U</math> is typically chosen as the complement of a ray or curve in the complex plane going from 0 (inclusive) to infinity in some direction. In this case, the curve is known as a [[branch cut]]. For example, the principal branch has a branch cut along the negative real axis.

If the function <math>\operatorname{L} (z)</math> is extended to be defined at a point of the branch cut, it will necessarily be discontinuous there; at best it will be continuous "on one side", like <math>\operatorname{Log} z</math> at a negative real number.

=== Power series for branches ===
Like every [[holomorphic function]], the complex logarithm can be represented locally – near any point in its domain – with a [[power series]]; that is, it is also [[analytic function|analytic]]. Because the logarithm is the integral of <math>1/z</math>, its power series can be found by term-by-term integration of a power series for <math>z \mapsto 1/z</math>. A power series for <math>z \mapsto 1/z</math>  centered at any point <math>z_0 \ne 0</math> can itself be found by considering <math>1/z</math> as the sum of a [[geometric series]] with initial term <math>1/z_0</math> and common ratio <math>(z-z_0)/(-z_0)</math>.{{cn|date=April 2026}}
<math display=block>
\frac{1}{z}
= \frac{1}{z_0} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - \dfrac{z-z_0}{-z_0}}
= \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{z_0} \left(\frac{z-z_0}{-z_0}\right)^n 
= \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{z_0^{n+1}} (z-z_0)^n.
</math>
This series converges in the disk <math>|z-z_0| < |z_0|</math>, the largest disk not containing the origin (where there is a [[Zeros and poles|pole]]). After term-by-term integration:
<math display=block>
\log z = \log z_0 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{nz_0^{n}} (z-z_0)^{n}.
</math>

=== Antiderivative - constant of power Series ===
The representation of <math>\tfrac{1}{z}</math> by a [[power series]] with the center <math>z_0\not=0</math> provides a [[Taylor series]] representation for a branch of the logarithm on <math>\overline{D_r(z_0)}</math> with <math>r< |z_0|</math> and <math>c= \ln(|z_0|) + i\cdot t</math> similar to the [[Mercator series]] with an arbitrary center <math>z_0=|z_0|\cdot e^{it} \not=0</math>:
<math display="block">
F(z)= c +
 \sum_{n=0}^\infty 
\frac{ (-1)^n }{z_0^{n+1} \cdot (n+1)}  \cdot (z-z_0)^{n+1} 
</math>
The corresponding branch of the logarithm for <math>F</math> is defined on the domain <math>U:= \C \setminus \{ z\in \C \, : \,  z=\lambda \cdot z_0 \mbox{ with } 0  \geq \lambda \in \R \}</math>.

=== Complex logarithm for negative real numbers ===
By removing the negative imaginary axis from the domain of the branch of the logarithm 
<math display="block">U_i:= \C \setminus \{ z\in \C \, : \,  z=\lambda \cdot i \mbox{ with } 0  \geq \lambda \in \R \}</math> 
a branch of the logarithm can be defined for all <math>x\in \R \setminus \{0\}</math> with:
<math display="block">\ln(-x) = \ln(x)+ i\cdot \pi </math> with <math>x \in \R</math> and <math>x < 0</math>.
The branch of the logarithm on <math>U_i</math> provides the standard logarithm <math>\ln(x)</math> for <math>x \in \R</math> and <math>x > 0</math>.

===The derivative of the complex logarithm===
Each branch <math>\operatorname{L} (z)</math> of <math>\log z</math> on an open set <math>U</math> is the inverse of a restriction of the exponential function, namely the restriction to the image <math>\operatorname{L} (U)</math>. Since the exponential function is [[Holomorphic function|holomorphic]] (that is, complex differentiable) with nonvanishing derivative, the complex analogue of the [[inverse function theorem]] applies. It shows that <math>\operatorname{L} (z)</math> is holomorphic on <math>U</math>, and <math>\operatorname{L}'(z) = 1/z</math> for each <math>z</math> in <math>U</math>.<ref name=Sarason /> Another way to prove this is to check the [[Cauchy–Riemann equations#Other representations|Cauchy–Riemann equations in polar coordinates]].<ref name=Sarason />

===Constructing branches via integration===
The function <math>\ln(x)</math> for real <math>x > 0</math> can be constructed by the formula
<math display="block">\ln(x) = \int_1^x \frac{du}{u}.</math>
If the range of integration started at a positive number <math>a</math> other than 1, the formula would have to be
<math display="block">\ln(x) = \ln(a) + \int_a^x \frac{du}{u}</math>
instead.

In developing the analogue for the ''complex'' logarithm, there is an additional complication: the definition of the [[complex integral]] requires a choice of path. Fortunately, if the integrand is holomorphic, then the value of the integral is unchanged by [[homotopy|deforming the path]] (while holding the endpoints fixed), and in a [[simply connected]] region <math>U</math> (a region with "no holes"), ''any'' path from <math>a</math> to <math>z</math> inside <math>U</math> can be [[homotopy|continuously deformed]] inside <math>U</math> into any other. All this leads to the following:

{{block indent | left = 1.6 | text = <p>If <math>U</math> is a simply connected open subset of <math>\mathbb{C}</math> not containing 0, then a branch of <math>\log z</math> defined on <math>U</math> can be constructed by choosing a starting point <math>a</math> in <math>U</math>, choosing a logarithm <math>b</math> of <math>a</math>, and defining <math display="block">L(z) = b + \int_a^z \frac{dw}{w}</math> for each <math>z</math> in <math>U</math>.<ref>Lang, p. 121.</ref></p>}}

==The complex logarithm as a conformal map==
[[Image:Logez02.jpg|200px|right|thumb|The circles {{math|1=Re(Log ''z'') =}} constant and the rays {{math|1=Im(Log&nbsp;''z'') =}} constant in the complex {{mvar|z}}-plane.]]
[[File:Complex log mapping.svg|thumb|right|Complex log mapping maps radii to horizontal lines and circles to vertical lines]]
Any holomorphic map <math>f\colon U \to \mathbb{C}</math> satisfying <math>f'(z) \ne 0</math> for all <math>z \in U</math> is a [[conformal map]], which means that if two curves passing through a point <math>a</math> of <math>U</math> form an angle <math>\alpha</math> (in the sense that the [[tangent line]]s to the curves at <math>a</math> form an angle <math>\alpha</math>), then the images of the two curves form the ''same'' angle <math>\alpha</math> at <math>f(a)</math>.
Since a branch of <math>\log z</math> is holomorphic, and since its derivative <math>1/z</math> is never 0, it defines a conformal map.

For example, the principal branch <math>w = \operatorname{Log} z</math>, viewed as a mapping from <math>\mathbb{C}-\mathbb{R}_{\le 0}</math> to the horizontal strip defined by <math>\left| \operatorname{Im}z \right| < \pi</math>, has the following properties, which are direct consequences of the formula in terms of polar form:
* Circles<ref>Strictly speaking, the point on each circle on the negative real axis should be discarded, or the principal value should be used there.</ref> in the {{mvar|z}}-plane centered at 0 are mapped to vertical segments in the {{mvar|w}}-plane connecting <math>a - \pi i</math> to <math>a + \pi i</math>, where <math>a</math> is the real log of the radius of the circle.
* Rays emanating from 0 in the {{mvar|z}}-plane are mapped to horizontal lines in the {{mvar|w}}-plane.

Each circle and ray in the {{mvar|z}}-plane as above meet at a [[right angle]]. Their images under Log are a vertical segment and a horizontal line (respectively) in the {{mvar|w}}-plane, and these too meet at a right angle. This is an illustration of the conformal property of Log.

==The associated Riemann surface==
[[Image:Riemann surface log.svg|thumb|right|A visualization of the Riemann surface of {{math|log&nbsp;''z''}}. The surface appears to spiral around a vertical line corresponding to the origin of the complex plane. The actual surface extends arbitrarily far both horizontally and vertically, but is cut off in this image.]]

===Construction===
The various branches of <math>\log z</math> cannot be glued to give a single continuous function <math>\log \colon \mathbb{C}^* \to \mathbb{C}</math> because two branches may give different values at a point where both are defined. Compare, for example, the principal branch <math>\operatorname{Log} z</math> on <math>\mathbb{C}-\mathbb{R}_{\le 0}</math> with imaginary part <math>\theta</math> in <math>(-\pi, \pi)</math> and the branch <math>\operatorname{L} (z)</math> on <math>\mathbb{C}-\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}</math> whose imaginary part <math>\theta</math> lies in <math>(0, 2 \pi)</math>. These agree on the [[upper half plane]], but not on the lower half plane. So it makes sense to glue the domains of these branches ''only along the copies of the upper half plane''. The resulting glued domain is connected, but it has two copies of the lower half plane. Those two copies can be visualized as two levels of a parking garage, and one can get from the <math>\text{Log}</math> level of the lower half plane up to the <math>\text{L}</math> level of the lower half plane by going <math>2 \pi</math> radians counterclockwise around {{math|0}}, first crossing the positive real axis (of the <math>\text{Log}</math> level) into the shared copy of the upper half plane and then crossing the negative real axis (of the <math>\text{L}</math> level) into the <math>\text{L}</math> level of the lower half plane.

One can continue by gluing branches with imaginary part <math>\theta</math> in <math>(\pi, 3 \pi)</math>, in <math>(2 \pi, 4 \pi)</math>, and so on, and in the other direction, branches with imaginary part <math>\theta</math> in <math>(-2 \pi, 0)</math>, in <math>(-3 \pi, -\pi)</math>, and so on. The final result is a connected surface that can be viewed as a spiraling parking garage with infinitely many levels extending both upward and downward. This is the Riemann surface <math>R</math> associated to <math>\log z</math>.<ref>Ahlfors, Section&nbsp;4.3.</ref>

A point on <math>R</math> can be thought of as a pair <math>(z, \theta)</math> where <math>\theta</math> is a possible value of the argument of <math>z</math>. In this way, {{mvar|R}} can be embedded in <math>\mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{R} \approx \mathbb{R}^3</math>.

===The logarithm function on the Riemann surface===
Because the domains of the branches were glued only along open sets where their values agreed, the branches glue to give a single well-defined function <math>\log_R \colon R \to \mathbb{C}</math>.<ref>The notations {{math|''R''}} and {{math|log<sub>''R''</sub>}} are not universally used.</ref> It maps each point <math>(z, \theta)</math> on <math>R</math> to <math>\ln |z| + i \theta</math>. This process of extending the original branch <math>\text{Log}</math> by gluing compatible holomorphic functions is known as [[analytic continuation]].

There is a "projection map" from <math>R</math> down to <math>\mathbb{C}^*</math> that "flattens" the spiral, sending <math>(z, \theta)</math> to <math>z</math>. For any <math>z \in \mathbb{C}^*</math>, if one takes all the points <math>(z, \theta)</math> of <math>R</math> lying "directly above" <math>z</math> and evaluates <math>\log_R</math> at all these points, one gets all the logarithms of <math>z</math>.

=== Gluing all branches of log z ===
Instead of gluing only the branches chosen above, one can start with ''all'' branches of <math>\log z</math>, and simultaneously glue ''every'' pair of branches <math>L_1\colon U_1 \to \mathbb{C}</math> and <math>L_2\colon U_2 \to \mathbb{C}</math> along the largest open subset of <math>U_1 \cap U_2</math> on which <math>L_1</math> and <math>L_2</math> agree. This yields the same Riemann surface <math>R</math> and function <math>\log_R</math> as before. This approach, although slightly harder to visualize, is more natural in that it does not require selecting any particular branches.

If <math>U'</math> is an open subset of <math>R</math> projecting bijectively to its image <math>U</math> in <math>\mathbb{C}^*</math>, then the restriction of <math>\log_R</math> to <math>U'</math> corresponds to a branch of <math>\log z</math> defined on <math>U</math>. Every branch of <math>\log z</math> arises in this way.

===The Riemann surface as a universal cover===
The projection map <math>R \to \mathbb{C}^*</math> realizes <math>R</math> as a [[covering space]] of <math>\mathbb{C}^*</math>. In fact, it is a [[Galois covering]] with [[deck transformation]] group isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>, generated by the [[homeomorphism]] sending <math>(z, \theta)</math> to <math>(z, \theta+2\pi)</math>.

As a [[complex manifold]], <math>R</math> is [[biholomorphic]] with <math>\mathbb{C}</math> via <math>\log_R</math>. (The inverse map sends <math>z</math> to <math>\left(e^z, \operatorname{Im}(z)\right)</math>.) This shows that <math>R</math> is simply connected, so <math>R</math> is the [[universal cover]] of <math>\mathbb{C}^*</math>.

==Applications==
* The complex logarithm is needed to define [[exponentiation#Complex exponentiation|exponentiation]] in which the base is a complex number. Namely, if <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are complex numbers with <math>a \not = 0</math>, one can use the principal value to define <math>a^b = e^{b \operatorname{Log} a}</math>. One can also replace <math>\operatorname{Log}a</math> by other logarithms of <math>a</math> to obtain other values of <math>a^b</math>, differing by factors of the form <math>e^{2\pi i nb}</math>.<ref name=Ahlfors/><ref>Kreyszig, p.&nbsp;640.</ref>  The expression <math>a^b</math> has a single value [[if and only if]] <math>b</math> is an integer.<ref name=Ahlfors/>
* Because [[trigonometric functions]] can be expressed as [[rational functions]] of <math>e^{iz}</math>, the [[inverse trigonometric functions#Logarithmic forms|inverse trigonometric functions]] can be expressed in terms of complex logarithms.
* In electrical engineering, the [[propagation constant]] involves a complex logarithm.

==Generalizations==
===Logarithms to other bases===
Just as for real numbers, one can define for complex numbers <math>b</math> and <math>x</math>
<math display="block">\log_b x = \frac{\log x}{\log b},</math>
with the only caveat that its value depends on the choice of a branch of log defined at <math>b</math> and <math>x</math> (with <math>\log b \not = 0</math>). For example, using the principal value gives
<math display="block">\log_i e = \frac{\operatorname{Log} e}{\operatorname{Log} i} = \frac1{\pi i/2} = -\frac{2i}{\pi}.</math>

===Logarithms of holomorphic functions===
If <math>f</math> is a holomorphic function on a connected open subset <math>U</math> of <math>\mathbb{C}</math>, then a branch of <math>\log f</math> on <math>U</math> is a continuous function <math>g</math> on <math>U</math> such that <math>e^{g(z)} = f(z)</math> for all <math>z</math> in <math>U</math>. Such a function <math>g</math> is necessarily holomorphic with <math>g'(z) = f'(z)/f(z)</math> for all <math>z</math> in <math>U</math>.

If <math>U</math> is a simply connected open subset of <math>\mathbb{C}</math>, and <math>f</math> is a nowhere-vanishing holomorphic function on <math>U</math>, then a branch of <math>\log f</math> defined on <math>U</math> can be constructed by choosing a starting point <math>a</math> in <math>U</math>, choosing a logarithm <math>b</math> of <math>f(a)</math>, and defining
<math display="block">g(z) = b + \int_a^z \frac{f'(w)}{f(w)}\,dw</math>
for each <math>z</math> in <math>U</math>.<ref name=Sarason/>
